details:
**Dismembered into fourteen pieces by Set**
Osiris's jealous brother Set (Seth) murdered him and cut his body into fourteen pieces, which he scattered across Egypt or threw into the Nile. His wife Isis, often helped by her sister Nephthys, searched for and recovered thirteen of the pieces, then bound them back together, making Osiris the first mummy.

**Isis and Horus**
Isis is Osiris's sister-wife, who restored his body and briefly revived him (in some versions with a spell taught by their father Geb) so she could conceive their son Horus. Horus later avenged his father by battling Set for the throne of Egypt, and "father of Horus" and "husband of Isis" are the standard giveaways.

**Atef crown and crook and flail**
Osiris's signature regalia. The atef is a tall white crown flanked by two ostrich feathers, said to represent truth and justice (the feathers of Ma'at), and the crook and flail he holds across his chest symbolize kingship and his claim to the throne of Egypt.

**The chest or coffin thrown into the Nile**
Set tricked Osiris into lying down in a beautiful chest built exactly to his measurements, then shut the lid, sealed it with molten lead, and threw it into the Nile, where Osiris drowned. Plutarch says Set (Typhon) was helped by seventy-two accomplices and by Aso, a queen of Ethiopia.

**The tamarisk tree and palace at Byblos**
The coffin floated to Byblos in Phoenicia, where a tamarisk (or erica) tree grew around it. King Malcander (also spelled Malacander) cut down the tree and used its trunk as a pillar in his palace. Isis came to Byblos, worked as a nursemaid for the queen (Astarte in Plutarch), and tried to make the royal baby immortal by holding him in fire, much like Demeter at Eleusis, before she recovered the coffin.

**Djed pillar**
A pillar-shaped symbol of stability and continuity that represents Osiris's backbone. It is linked to the pillar at Byblos that held his body, which Isis anointed after retrieving it.

**Green (or black) skin**
Osiris is usually shown as a mummified king with green or black skin. The color stands for vegetation, fertility, the black silt left by the Nile floods, and his death and rebirth. He was also an agricultural god, and the grain god Neper is sometimes shown as wheat sprouting from his body.

**Eldest son of Geb and Nut**
Osiris was the first child of the earth god Geb and the sky goddess Nut. His siblings are Isis, Set, and Nephthys (and in some accounts Horus the Elder). In the myth recorded by Plutarch, the five siblings were born on five extra (intercalary) days that Thoth won from the moon god Khonsu in a game, because Ra had forbidden Nut to give birth on any day of the year.

**The fish that ate his phallus**
The one piece of Osiris that Isis never found was his phallus, which was eaten by fish, most often named as the oxyrhynchus (in some accounts a catfish or other species). For this reason priests of Osiris refused to eat fish. Isis fashioned a replacement phallus, sometimes described as golden, before she conceived Horus.

**Nephthys and the birth of Anubis**
Osiris fathered the jackal god Anubis with his sister Nephthys, Set's wife, who in many versions disguised herself as Isis. This affair is sometimes given as Set's motive for killing him. Nephthys nonetheless helped Isis search for Osiris's body and helped raise Horus, earning the title "nurse-mother."

**Serapis**
Under the Ptolemaic pharaohs, Osiris was combined with the Apis bull of Memphis to form the Greco-Egyptian god Serapis (Osiris-Apis). The Serapeum of Alexandria, the main center of Serapis's cult, was destroyed in 391 CE by a Christian mob led by Patriarch Theophilus.

**Ruler of the Duat and judge of the dead**
Osiris rules the Duat, the Egyptian underworld, and presides over the judgment of the dead. There, in the Hall of Two Truths, a dead person's heart is weighed against the feather of Ma'at. The pure go on to the Field of Reeds, while Ammit devours the hearts of the wicked. In many accounts Osiris took over the role of lord of the dead from Anubis.

**"Foremost of the Westerners" (Khenti-Amentiu)**
An epithet Osiris took after being merged with Khenti-Amentiu, the jackal god of the necropolis at Abydos, by the Middle Kingdom. The "West" refers to the land of the dead, since the sun sets in the west. He was also associated with Wepwawet, the "Opener of the Ways."

**Abydos and its festival**
Abydos was Osiris's chief cult center and his supposed burial place. It held a great temple and an annual festival, the Osiris mysteries, recorded on the Ikhernofret Stela, in which his image was carried on the Neshmet bark in a procession led by Wepwawet. Worshippers also made "Osiris gardens," beds of sprouting grain shaped like the god.

**Banebdjedet, the ram of Mendes**
Osiris's ba (soul) was worshipped at the city of Mendes as a sacred living ram called Banebdjedet. The Book of the Heavenly Cow identifies this ram god as Osiris's soul.
